title: Product life cycle

book.title: My Revision Notes: AQA A Level Design and Technology: Product Design

needs: Name the stages of the product life cycle and say what happens to sales in each.
Explain how extension strategies keep a product selling.
Explain demand pull and technology push, with an example of each.
Define planned obsolescence and give a more sustainable alternative.
Explain how products evolve through research and development (R&D).

doNow.q: What does the product life cycle chart?
doNow.a: A product's sales over time, from its introduction to its withdrawal.
Designing and making products that need replacing on a regular basis.
Mainstream products usable by as many people as reasonably possible, with no special adaptation.

doNow.q: What does the FSC scheme make sure of?
doNow.a: That timber is used sustainably: it comes from responsibly managed sources.

clues: I was worn on the head.

chunks.label: Stages of the PLC
chunks.summary: A product's sales charted over time, from launch to withdrawal.

items.text: Charts a product's sales from introduction to withdrawal; plan its decline and replacement carefully.
Sales start low, then take off; launched with publicity after market research.
Advertising grows sales as consumers move to it from older products.
Sales peak; the aim is to keep the product here as long as possible.
Sales fall, as most people who want one have bought it; then it's withdrawn.
An updated, improved version is released to keep sales going.
Not the PLC: it follows a product's environmental impact, not its sales.

parts.name: Introduction
parts.text: Launched with publicity; sales start to take off.

parts.name: Maturity
parts.text: Peak sales, kept for as long as possible.

parts.name: Decline
parts.text: Sales fall; the product is eventually withdrawn.

parts.name: Replacement
parts.text: An updated, improved version keeps sales going.

check.q: What happens to sales in the maturity stage?
check.a: They peak; the company tries to keep the product there as long as possible.

check.q: Why is an updated version released at the end of the life cycle?
check.a: To maintain sales as the original product declines.

chunks.label: Extension strategies
chunks.summary: Updating or redesigning a product to keep it selling.

items.text: Updating or redesigning a product to maintain its sales.
The Apple iPhone and Samsung Galaxy use extension strategies to keep selling.
Redesigned 11 times in 50 years to keep it selling.
New materials, updated electronics, new styling, better sustainability or user experience.

check.q: Give an example of a product that uses an extension strategy.
check.a: The Toyota Corolla (redesigned 11 times in 50 years), the Apple iPhone or the Samsung Galaxy.

check.q: Name two ways a product can be refreshed.
check.a: Any two: new materials, updated electronics, new styling, improved sustainability, a redesigned user experience.

chunks.label: Demand pull
chunks.summary: Consumers want features, and designers respond.

items.text: Consumers' demand for desirable features, which product designers often respond to.
Smartphone users want batteries that last longer, so designers improve them.
Users want phones that store more, so memory gets larger.

check.a: Demand by consumers for desirable features.

check.q: Give an example of demand pull in a smartphone.
check.a: Improved battery life or larger memory.

chunks.label: Technology push
chunks.summary: New technology or materials come first; designers then find products to use them in.

items.text: New technology or materials are developed, and designers find ways to use them in new or improved products.
The cost of research and development drives companies to push new ideas.
Not driven by consumer demand, so it may not sell: consumers have to be sold its merits.
A head-mounted computer that failed: not worth the cost, with safety and privacy worries.

check.q: Why isn't technology push always successful?
check.a: It isn't driven by consumer demand, so consumers may not be convinced it's worth buying, as with Google Glass.
Consumers weren't convinced it was worth the expense, and there were concerns over safety and privacy.

chunks.label: Planned obsolescence
chunks.summary: Products designed to need replacing regularly.

items.text: Designing and making products that need replacing on a regular basis.
Parts stop being available, so the product can't be repaired.
New software won't work with the product, so it has to be replaced.
Modular and upgradeable: a more customer-friendly, sustainable approach.

check.q: Give two factors that can make a product obsolete.
check.a: Spare parts are no longer available; software incompatibility.

check.q: Why is the Fairphone an alternative to planned obsolescence?
check.a: It is modular and upgradeable, a more customer-friendly and sustainable approach.

chunks.label: Evolution of products
chunks.summary: Gradual change driven by new technology, methods and materials.

items.text: Gradual change in products due to new technologies, manufacturing methods and materials.
Explore and develop new ideas for products.
Research and development is very expensive: Apple spent $2.5 billion in 2016.
R&D brought LED, OLED, HDR, 4K (UHD), curved screens and smart features.
R&D brought more pixels, faster firing, Wi-Fi, water resistance and an articulated screen.

check.a: New technologies, manufacturing methods and materials, explored by R&D departments.

check.q: Give two features R&D has added to televisions.
check.a: Any two: LED, OLED, HDR, 4K (UHD), a curved screen, smart capability.

keywords.def: The introduction, growth, maturity, decline and replacement of a product's sales.
The launch stage, when sales start to take off.
The stage when sales are at their peak.
The stage when sales fall until the product is withdrawn.
Updating or redesigning a product to maintain its sales.
Demand by consumers for desirable features.
New technology or materials are developed, then designers use them in new or improved products.
Designing products that need replacing on a regular basis.
Exploring and developing new ideas for products.
Gradual change due to new technologies, manufacturing methods and materials.

apply.q: Sales of a popular electric scooter have reached their peak and are starting to level off.
tools: Withdraw it from sale straight away
reasons: An extension strategy keeps sales going before the product declines
Sales have peaked, so there's no point carrying on
Customers will have to buy a new one sooner

apply.q: Customer reviews say a company's smartphone runs out of charge too quickly.
tools: Improve the battery life in the next model
Make the battery impossible to replace
reasons: Designers respond to demand pull: consumers' demand for desirable features
Any new feature from R&D will sell
It makes the phone need replacing more often
Consumers just need to be sold its merits

apply.q: A company wants its new phone to be more customer-friendly and sustainable than phones that are replaced when one part fails.
tools: Stop supplying spare parts after two years
Make it incompatible with older software
A new colour for each model
reasons: Parts can be upgraded instead of replacing the whole phone, as with the Fairphone
Customers will need to replace it regularly
It pushes customers to buy the latest model
It keeps the product looking new

apply.q: A company's R&D department has developed a head-mounted display that no customer has asked for.
tools: Convince consumers of its merits before launch
Assume it will sell because it's new
Wait for consumers to ask for it
reasons: With technology push, consumers need to be sold the merits of new ideas
R&D is cheap, so there's little risk
Demand pull means customers already want it

items.why: The only one that failed to convince consumers.

order.q: Put the stages of the product life cycle in order.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order of the product life cycle?
quiz.why: Sales take off after launch, grow, peak, then fall, and an updated version replaces the product.

quiz.q: In which stage are a product's sales at their peak?
quiz.why: Companies try to keep the product in maturity for as long as possible.

quiz.q: In the decline stage, most consumers who wanted the product have already bought it.
quiz.why: Sales fall and the product is eventually withdrawn.

quiz.q: What helps sales grow in the evolution and growth stage?
quiz.why: Advertising helps sales grow as consumers move to the product from older ones.

quiz.q: The product life cycle is the same as a life-cycle assessment of a product's environmental impact.
quiz.why: The PLC tracks sales; a life-cycle assessment follows environmental impacts.

quiz.q: Why is an updated, improved version released at the end of a product's life cycle?
options: To make the old version easier to repair
quiz.why: The replacement keeps sales going as the original declines.

quiz.q: The Toyota Corolla has been redesigned 11 times in 50 years.
quiz.why: It's an example of an extension strategy.

quiz.q: What is an extension strategy?
options: Updating or redesigning a product to maintain its sales
Making a product need replacing regularly
Marketing a new invention nobody asked for
quiz.why: Extension strategies keep a product selling, as with smartphones and the Toyota Corolla.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of a product kept selling by extension strategies?
quiz.why: New iPhone and Samsung Galaxy models keep these smartphones selling.

quiz.q: What is demand pull?
options: Demand by consumers for desirable features
Designers using newly developed technology or materials
quiz.why: Product designers often respond to it.

quiz.q: Improved battery life in a smartphone is an example of demand pull.
quiz.why: Consumers want it, and designers respond. Larger memory is another example.

quiz.q: What is technology push?
options: New technology or materials are developed, and designers find ways to use them in new or improved products.
Redesigning a product to maintain sales
quiz.why: It isn't driven by consumer demand, so the products may not sell.

quiz.q: Technology push products always sell well because they are new.
quiz.why: It isn't driven by consumer demand, so consumers have to be sold the merits; Google Glass failed.

quiz.q: Why did Google Glass fail?
options: Consumers weren't convinced it was worth the expense, and there were safety and privacy concerns
Its spare parts stopped being available
Its battery life was improved too late
quiz.why: It shows that technology push isn't always successful.

quiz.q: What is planned obsolescence?
options: Designing and making products that need replacing regularly
Redesigning a product to maintain its sales
Responding to consumers' demand for features
quiz.why: Products are designed to need replacing on a regular basis.

quiz.q: Which of these could make a product obsolete?
options: Spare parts are no longer available
quiz.why: Unavailable spare parts and software incompatibility are both factors.

quiz.q: The Fairphone is modular and upgradeable.
quiz.why: It's a more customer-friendly, sustainable approach than planned obsolescence.

quiz.q: What causes the gradual evolution of products?
options: New technologies, manufacturing methods and materials
quiz.why: R&D departments explore and develop these new ideas.

quiz.q: Research and development is cheap for large companies.
quiz.why: R&D is very expensive, even for companies such as Apple.

quiz.q: R&D departments explore and develop new ideas, such as OLED screens and HDR for televisions.
quiz.why: Evolutionary features like these are introduced by R&D.

written.q: A company launches a new electric toothbrush. Describe what happens to its sales through the stages of its product life cycle.
points: Introduction: it is launched with publicity after market research, and sales start to take off.
Evolution and growth: advertising helps sales grow as consumers move to it from older products.
Maturity: sales peak, and the company tries to keep it there as long as possible.
Decline: most people who want one have bought it, so sales fall and it is eventually withdrawn.
Replacement: an updated, improved version is released to maintain sales.
written.model: In the introduction stage the toothbrush is launched with publicity, following market research, and sales start to take off. During evolution and growth, advertising helps sales grow as consumers move to it from older toothbrushes. In maturity sales are at their peak, and the company tries to keep them there for as long as possible. In decline, most people who want one have already bought it, so sales fall and it is eventually withdrawn. To maintain sales, an updated, improved version is released as its replacement.
written.note: 1 mark per stage named with what happens to sales, up to 4.

written.q: Explain the difference between demand pull and technology push.
points: Demand pull comes from consumers demanding desirable features, such as longer battery life in a smartphone.
Technology push starts with new technology or materials, which designers find ways to use in new or improved products; it isn't driven by consumer demand, so it may not sell, such as Google Glass.
written.model: Demand pull starts with consumers: designers respond to their demand for desirable features, such as longer battery life in a smartphone. Technology push starts with new technology or materials, which designers find ways to use in new or improved products. It isn't driven by consumer demand, so it may not sell, as Google Glass showed.

written.q: Compare planned obsolescence with the modular, upgradeable approach of the Fairphone.
points: Planned obsolescence designs and makes products that need replacing on a regular basis…
…for example because spare parts stop being available or software becomes incompatible.
The Fairphone is modular and upgradeable…
…so it is a more customer-friendly and sustainable approach.
With planned obsolescence the whole product has to be replaced; the Fairphone is designed to be upgraded instead.
written.model: Planned obsolescence means designing and making products that need replacing on a regular basis, for example because spare parts stop being available or the product becomes incompatible with new software. The Fairphone takes the opposite approach: it is modular and upgradeable, so it is designed to be upgraded rather than replaced, which is more customer-friendly and sustainable.
written.note: 1 mark per point, with at least one point on each, up to 4.

written.q: Explain how extension strategies can keep a product selling. Use an example.
points: An extension strategy updates or redesigns a product to maintain its sales…
…so an updated, improved version replaces it before it declines.
It can be refreshed with new materials, updated electronics, new styling, better sustainability or a redesigned user experience.
Example: smartphones such as the Apple iPhone and Samsung Galaxy.
Example: the Toyota Corolla, redesigned 11 times in 50 years.
written.model: An extension strategy updates or redesigns a product to maintain its sales, so an updated, improved version takes over before the original declines. The product can be refreshed with new materials, updated electronics or new styling. For example, the Toyota Corolla has been redesigned 11 times in 50 years to keep it selling.
written.note: 1 mark per point or explanation, up to 4; the example is needed for full marks.

written.q: Evaluate the benefits and drawbacks for a company of developing new products through technology push.
points: R&D departments explore and develop new ideas for products.
New technologies drive the gradual evolution of products, such as OLED, HDR and 4K in televisions.
R&D is very expensive, and that cost leads companies to push new ideas.
It isn't driven by consumer demand, so consumers have to be sold the merits of new ideas and features.
New developments aren't always popular: Google Glass failed over its cost and concerns about safety and privacy.
Demand pull, by contrast, responds to features consumers already want, such as longer battery life.
Justified conclusion, e.g. technology push can lead product evolution, but only if consumers can be convinced the new feature is worth it.
written.model: With technology push, new technology or materials are developed and designers find ways to use them in new or improved products: R&D departments explore new ideas, and new technologies drive the evolution of products, as with OLED, HDR and 4K in televisions. However, R&D is very expensive, and because technology push isn't driven by consumer demand, consumers have to be sold the merits of each new idea. New developments aren't always popular: Google Glass failed because consumers weren't convinced it was worth the expense, and there were concerns over safety and privacy. Demand pull, by contrast, responds to features consumers already want. Technology push can lead the evolution of products, but it only pays off if the company can convince consumers the new feature is worth it.
written.note: Tick the points made, then use the levels under the model answer to decide the mark.

levels.text: Detailed, balanced points on both sides, with a justified conclusion.
Some points, mostly on one side, or a conclusion that isn't justified.

written.q: Explain why a product's sales fall in the decline stage of its life cycle.
points: Most consumers who wanted the product have already bought it.
Changing technology, fashion or regulation, or replacement products, reduce demand.
written.model: Sales fall because most consumers who wanted the product have already bought it. Demand also drops as technology, fashion or regulations change, or as replacement products arrive.
